title: 245-Million-Year-Old Fossil Reveals Oldest Known Reptile Digestive System
summary: A fossil from China is giving scientists an incredibly detailed look inside a marine reptile that swam the seas about 245 million years ago. The specimen, named Austronaga minuta, is nearly complete — and it preserves not just bones, but also large parts of its digestive system. Researchers identified a stomach, liver and intestines. It's the oldest known example of a largely complete digestive system in a reptile. The findings were published in Science Advances. Austronaga was small — only about 60 centimeters long — but its body was built for swimming. It had an unusually long neck and tail. Its long tail likely provided propulsion, while its extended, fin-like front legs helped with steering. Its hind legs were much smaller and probably didn't help much with swimming. What's surprising is that Austronaga wasn't closely related to famous marine reptiles like ichthyosaurs or mosasaurs. Instead, it was related to land-dwelling archosaurs — the group that includes crocodiles and dinosaurs. "The archosaurs and their ancestors were the most diverse group of reptiles on land during the time of the dinosaurs, but we always thought that their adaptation to life in the sea was limited," said Dr. Stephan Spiekman, a paleontologist at the State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart and co-author of the study. "However, the discovery of Austronaga shows that early representatives of this lineage had already developed complex adaptations to life in the oceans." The digestive system itself was surprisingly simple. "While today's birds and crocodiles have a two-part stomach, Austronaga had only a single stomach chamber," explained Dr. Nick Fraser of the National Museums Scotland. "This shows that the stomachs of archosaurs were initially quite simple and only evolved later." The fossil is now in Beijing, and researchers hope future discoveries will reveal more about how reptiles adapted to ocean life.
why_it_matters: Studying how an ancient reptile's body was built shows students how evolution works step by step — and it proves that one lucky fossil can overturn what textbooks say about an entire group of animals, so scientific ideas are always open to revision.

background_read: The fossil comes from rocks about 245 million years old, a time when Earth was recovering from the Permian-Triassic mass extinction (the biggest die-off in Earth's history, when most species in the oceans disappeared). With so much empty ocean habitat, reptiles quickly spread into the seas.

Fossils that keep soft organs are extremely rare. Soft tissue usually rots or gets eaten before it can be buried and turned to stone, so most fossils are only bones, teeth or shells. That is why a specimen with a stomach, liver and intestines still visible is so valuable.

Science Advances (a scientific journal that publishes peer-reviewed research) printed the study. Co-author Stephan Spiekman works at the State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart in Germany, and Nick Fraser works at the National Museums Scotland (Scotland's national museum collection).

Ichthyosaurs and mosasaurs were two different groups of reptiles that also moved into the oceans — ichthyosaurs during the age of dinosaurs, mosasaurs much later. Austronaga belonged to neither of them; it sat on the archosaur branch, the same side of the family tree that today includes birds and crocodiles.

perspectives.description: This fossil shows that archosaurs, long thought of as mainly land animals, had already developed complex adaptations for life in the oceans — including a fin-like steering system and a swimming tail.
One specimen cannot tell us how common these adaptations were. Because soft tissue almost never fossilizes, the record is patchy, so the team's conclusions rest on a single lucky find.
The discovery fits a wider pattern: many unrelated reptile groups independently evolved similar swimming bodies and lifestyles when they moved into the sea, a process called convergent evolution.

More fossils from the same region and time period could show whether marine archosaurs were rare exceptions or a common feature of early Triassic oceans, and whether stomachs with two chambers appeared gradually.
